texte: I recommend structuring your rules so they are something you can programmatically extract, rather than embed into the content. Reason being is because a pattern has emerged for a rules shadow agent, which will use a rules corpus to gate commits. You probably haven't seen it yet, but a few months from now and everyone will be talking about it. The rules section of your document sets you up for generating the rules corpus that the shadow agent can load into context and view your diff and compare against the corpus. Also Skills are just context files. You don't really need to make skills when context is retrievable using standard bash/read tools.. Skills should be reserved for something that enables a capability, not for simply loading context.

Solid breakdown of Anthropic's skill authoring guide. The seven points are all real, and the structural ones (references one level deep, a TOC in any file over 100 lines, scripts for anything that can't vary) are worth applying to every skill people already have.
One correction for anyone watching, though: the head -100 part is framed as what Claude always does with reference files, but the doc actually says Claude may partially read a file when it's referenced from another referenced file, and might use something like head -100 to preview it in that case. So it's a nested-references problem, not default behavior. And "everything you know is outdated" is doing a lot of work in that title — these read as additions to the existing best practices, not a rewrite. Still a useful summary.

This feels like a leaky abstraction wrapped in cargo cult advice. Anthropic should handle indexing, partial reads and model-specific formatting rather than make users accommodate those quirks. And framing every update as “the rules have changed, go fix all your skills” breeds unnecessary FOMO. Focus on clear intent, meaningful constraints and what success looks like; use the current guidance where it solves an actual problem, rather than continually rebuilding around implementation quirks that will change again in 1–6 months. Skills should capture durable knowledge, not become a maintenance treadmill chasing the prompting advice of the week.
